title: Publish after the payment commits
dek: Moving a notification past the commit boundary prevents one false signal, but does not make payment and delivery atomic.
meta: Fictional change · Source and supplied in-memory probe results
footer: Based on the supplied source and probes. No real database or process-kill simulation is included.

sections.title: Two operations, one transaction callback
sections.content:
Lantern Ledger marks a payment paid and publishes a notification. Originally, both awaited operations ran inside the database transaction callback. The database stages the payment write, then commits only after the callback fulfills.

That placement does not bring publication into the transaction. publish is an external operation: rolling back database writes cannot retract a notification that has already escaped.

sections.title: A notification could outlive a failed commit
sections.content:
If publication succeeded and the later commit failed, the original function left the payment unpaid but sent one notification. The supplied probe records exactly that sequence: begin, write, publish, rollback.

Publication itself can also reject after producing a visible notification. In the original function, that rejection rolls back the payment while the notification remains. The author's atomicity claim therefore needs a narrower reading: changing the order can prevent publication after a failed commit, but cannot make the two operations succeed together.

sections.title: Await the commit before publishing
sections.content:
The changed function waits for the transaction itself, rather than publishing inside its callback:

{{CODE:0}}

Under the supplied contract, that first await completes only after commit. A write or commit rejection exits before publish. Publication failure now leaves the payment committed.

The probe models the two possible publication failures explicitly:

{{CODE:1}}

The counter represents an externally visible notification. Recorded results leave the changed payment paid in both cases, with zero notifications before the increment and one afterward. These are in-memory observations; the supplied verification file records no separate findings.

sections.title: Commit first is an ordering guarantee
sections.content: The change prevents notifications for failed commits. It still allows a committed payment without a notification if publication fails or the process stops between operations. No durable outbox or background retry closes that gap. Retrying an ambiguous publication can duplicate delivery: markPaid is idempotent, but publication has no deduplication guarantee. The concurrent probe produces two notifications in both versions. Payment and notification remain separate outcomes.
